entry.title: Building a 3D Zombie Survival Horror in Unity: Day 1 of Our Journey
entry.summary:
🧟‍♂️ The Road of the Dead: A New Indie Horror Adventure
Hi everyone! I’m a 12-year-old developer and today I’m officially starting a big project with my friend and classmate, Dardan. We decided to stop just playing games and start building our own. Our game is a 3D Survival Horror. The core idea is simple but intense: The Car is your Armor: It has its own HP. If the zombies damage it too much, it breaks down. The Switch: When the car stops, you HAVE to get out. That’s when the game changes from a driving simulator to a third-person survival fight against scary bosses. We’ve split the roles to work like a real indie studio: Me (Lead Programmer): I’m handling the C# scripts, the car physics, and the health systems using Unity. Dardan (Lead Designer): He’s in charge of the 3D models, environment design, and making the monsters look terrifying. We are developing this project using Unity (URP). Dell Latitude 7290. It’s a great challenge to optimize a 3D game for mobile-grade hardware, but it teaches me a lot about performance! Right now, I’ve just finished the basic car movement script and a simple health system. Dardan is working on the first "Scary Boss" model. We know we have a lot to learn, but we are excited! What do you think about the "Car HP" mechanic? Any tips for a young dev team starting with Unity?

entry.title: How to Secure AI Agents Against Authorization Attacks
entry.summary: Your AI agent is now an authorization boundary. If you haven't designed it that way, an attacker can use the agent's reasoning to perform actions your credentials were never supposed to allow. The Problem AI agents fail at authorization in a specific way: they can be prompted into translating an instruction they received at high privilege into an action that executes with whatever credentials the agent holds — regardless of whether those credentials are appropriate for the requested action. This isn't a traditional privilege escalation. The agent isn't breaking an access control. It's reasoning about the request and taking what it believes is the right action, using the permissions it has.
